hints: Output goes through `std::cout` with the `<<` operator, and the text goes in double quotes.
std::cout << "Welcome to C++!\n";
lessons.title: Welcome to C++
concept: C++ started at Bell Labs in 1979 as Bjarne Stroustrup's extension to C — nowadays a language of its own.
`std::cout` is the standard output stream. The `<<` operator inserts values into it, and `\n` inside a string moves output to a new line.
lessons.challenge: Print exactly: **Welcome to C++!** — this is fig. 1.2 from your slides.

hints: Start the counter at 0 and keep looping while it is less than 5.
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) std::cout << i << "\n";
lessons.title: Declare anywhere
concept: Unlike C, C++ lets you declare variables where you need them — not just at the top of a block.
That includes the `for` header: `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)`. The counter exists only during the loop, then goes away.
lessons.example:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
    std::cout << i << "\n";   // prints 0, 1, 2
lessons.challenge: Using a counter declared in the loop header, print the numbers 0 through 4, one per line.

hints: Store the comparison in the bool: `result = a < b;`
std::cout << std::boolalpha << result << "\n"; — or use if/else to print the words.
lessons.title: The bool type
concept: C had no true/false type; C++ adds `bool` with literals `true` and `false`.
Relational operators like `<` produce bool values. `std::boolalpha` makes cout print them as words instead of 1/0.
lessons.example:
bool ok = (3 < 5);                     // true
std::cout << std::boolalpha << ok;     // prints: true
lessons.challenge: Read two integers `a` and `b`. Print **true** if `a < b`, otherwise **false**.

hints: Read into the fields directly: `std::cin >> p.x >> p.y;`
lessons.title: Tagged structs
concept: In C++ a struct tag is a type name by itself — you write `MyType v;`, no `struct` keyword needed at the declaration.
This is the first step toward classes: data grouped under one name, fields accessed with `.`
lessons.challenge: A `Point` struct is defined for you. Read `x` and `y`, store them in a Point, and print it as **(x, y)** — parenthesis, comma, space.

hints: You need three `\n` total — and two of them are next to each other.

std::cout << "Welcome
to

C++!

lessons.title: Escape sequences
concept: One statement can print several lines: `\n` is a newline wherever it appears in the string.
Two `\n` in a row produce a blank line.
lessons.challenge: Reproduce fig. 1.5 exactly — print **Welcome**, **to**, a blank line, then **C++!** using a single output statement.

hints: Chain the reads: `std::cin >> integer1 >> integer2;`
sum = integer1 + integer2; std::cout << "Sum is " << sum << std::endl;
lessons.title: Adding two integers
concept: `std::cin >> x` waits for input and stores it in `x`, converting to the variable's type. `=` assigns a value.
Insertions can be chained: `cout << "Sum is " << sum << endl;` — this is fig. 1.6 from your slides. (We skip the prompts; the grader only checks output.)
lessons.challenge: Read two integers and print **Sum is** followed by their total.

hints: Two separate output lines — remember the `\n` between them.
std::cout << a / b << "\n" << a % b << "\n";
lessons.title: Integer arithmetic
concept: Integer division truncates: `7 / 5` is `1`. The modulus operator `%` gives the remainder: `7 % 5` is `2`.
Precedence: parentheses first, then `* / %`, then `+ -`, applied left to right.
lessons.challenge: Read two integers `a` and `b`. Print `a / b` on the first line and `a % b` on the second.

hints: Six separate if statements, one per operator — each phrased exactly like the first.
The middle text for each: " is not equal to ", " is less than ", " is greater than ", " is less than or equal to ", " is greater than or equal to ".

lessons.title: Relational operators
concept: `using std::cout;` lets you drop the `std::` prefix for that name.
Equality (`==`, `!=`) and relational (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`) operators each produce a bool an `if` can test. Several relationships can hold at once.
lessons.example:
if (num1 == num2)
    cout << num1 << " is equal to " << num2 << endl;
lessons.challenge: Fig. 1.14: read two integers and print one line for **every** relationship that holds, in this order: equal, not equal, less than, greater than, less than or equal, greater than or equal. Match the slide's wording: e.g. **22 is greater than 12**.

hints: "At least 60" means `>= 60` — 60 itself passes.
cout << (grade >= 60 ? "Passed" : "Failed") << "\n";
lessons.title: if / else
concept: The selection structure chooses between paths. From the slides: *if grade is greater than or equal to 60, print Passed, else print Failed.*
Only sequence, selection, and repetition are needed to express any algorithm (Bohm & Jacopini) — no gotos, mmm 'kay?
lessons.challenge: Read a grade. Print **Passed** if it is at least 60, otherwise **Failed**.

hints: Because earlier tests already ruled out higher grades, each `else if` only needs its lower bound.
Finish the ladder with a plain `else` (no condition) for F.
lessons.title: Nested if / else
concept: Chained `else if` tests multiple cases; once one condition is met, the rest are skipped — so test from highest to lowest.
lessons.challenge: Read a grade and print the letter, exactly as in section 2.6: 90+ is **A**, 80-89 **B**, 70-79 **C**, 60-69 **D**, below 60 **F**.

hints: Inside the loop: declare a grade, read it with cin, and add it to total.
After the loop: cout << "Class average is " << total / 10 << endl;
lessons.title: Counter-controlled repetition
concept: Case study 1 (fig. 2.7): a `while` loop repeats while its condition is true.
Counter-controlled repetition runs an exact number of times: initialize a total and a counter, loop, add each grade, increment the counter.
lessons.challenge: Read exactly **10** grades. Print **Class average is** followed by the integer average (integer division, just like the book).

hints: Integer / integer truncates — cast one side: `static_cast<double>(total) / gradeCounter`.
cout << "Class average is " << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << average << endl;
lessons.title: Sentinel-controlled repetition
concept: Case study 2 (fig. 2.9): when you don't know how many values are coming, loop until a **sentinel** value (here `-1`) signals the end.
The average of an unknown count needs a `double`, printed with `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision(2)` from `<iomanip>`.
lessons.challenge: Read grades until `-1`. Print **Class average is** with two decimals. If the first value is the sentinel, print **No grades were entered** instead.

hints: if (result == 1) passes = passes + 1; else failures = failures + 1;
After the two count lines: if (passes > 8) cout << "Raise tuition" << endl;
lessons.title: Boss: exam results
concept: Case study 3 (fig. 2.11), nested control structures: an `if/else` **inside** a `while` loop.
Process 10 exam results: `1` means pass, `2` means fail. Count each kind as you go.
lessons.challenge: After the loop print **Passed** and the count, then **Failed** and the count, each on its own line. If more than 8 students passed, print **Raise tuition** as a third line.

hints: The `&` in `int &result` means result IS the caller's variable. Assigning to it changes theirs.
bool halve(int n, int &result) { if (n % 2 == 0) { result = n / 2; return true; } return false; }
lessons.title: Reference parameters
concept: Course functions return bool for success and hand results back through reference parameters, like `bool deleteFirst(KEY_VALUE &kv)`.
lessons.challenge: Write `bool halve(int n, int &result)`. If `n` is even, set `result` to `n / 2` and return **true**. If `n` is odd, leave `result` alone and return **false**.

hints: `int *a = new int[n];` allocates. Loop to fill, loop (or the same loop) to sum.
After printing: `delete[] a;` with the brackets, because it was allocated with `new[]`.
lessons.title: new and delete[]
concept: P1's list stores its data in `KEY_VALUE *keyValues = new KEY_VALUE[capacity]` and frees it with `delete[]` in the destructor.
lessons.challenge: Read `n`. Allocate an int array of size `n` with `new`, fill it so index `i` holds `i * i`, print the **sum** of the array, then free it with `delete[]`.

hints: Guard the loop with both conditions: `while (count < CAP && cin >> v && v != -1)`.
Store with `a[count] = v; count++;` then print count, capacity, and loop the values with spaces.
lessons.title: Count vs capacity
concept: Every ADT this semester tracks two numbers: `listCapacity` (room) and `listCount` (used). Confusing them is the classic P1 bug.
lessons.challenge: An array has capacity 8. Read integers until **-1** or until the array is **full**. Then print `count=C capacity=8` on one line and the stored values on the next.

hints: Constructor: `Counter::Counter() { n = 0; }` and bump is one line: `n = n + 1;`
The const goes in the definition too: `int Counter::get() const { return n; }`
lessons.title: Your first class
concept: A **class** bundles private data with the public functions allowed to touch it. Member functions are defined as `ClassName::functionName`.
lessons.challenge: Finish the `Counter` class: `Counter()` starts `n` at 0, `bump()` adds 1, and `get() const` returns `n`. The provided `main` bumps `k` times and prints the count.

hints: Write the default only in the declaration; the definition is plain `Tank::Tank(int f) { fuel = f; }`.
Clamp inside use: `fuel = fuel - amt; if (fuel < 0) fuel = 0;`
lessons.title: Constructors with defaults
concept: P1's constructor is `list(unsigned int size = 100, unsigned int expandSize = 5)`. Callers who pass nothing get the defaults.
lessons.challenge: Finish the `Tank` class: `Tank(int f = 50)` stores starting fuel, `use(int amt)` burns fuel but never below 0, `getFuel() const` returns it. Main prints your tank after one `use`, then a **default** tank.

hints: Loop `for (int i = count; i > 0; i--) a[i] = a[i - 1];` walks backward so nothing is lost.
After the shift: `a[0] = v; count++;` then print with spaces.
lessons.title: Insert means shift right
concept: P1's `insert(kv)` puts the new value at index 0 after shifting every entry one slot right. Shift from the **end** toward the front or you overwrite data.
lessons.challenge: Read `n`, then `n` values into an array, then one value `v`. Insert `v` at the **front** by shifting, and print the whole list space separated.

hints: Shift left goes forward: `for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) a[i] = a[i + 1];`
Save `a[0]` into a variable BEFORE the shift, or the value is gone.
lessons.title: Delete means shift left
concept: P1's `deleteFirst(kv)` saves the first entry into the reference parameter, shifts everything left, and returns false on an empty list without touching `kv`.
lessons.challenge: Read `n`, then `n` values. If the list is empty print **empty**. Otherwise delete the first entry: print `deleted X`, then the remaining values on the next line.

hints: The guard is `if (i > count)`, not `>=`. Index equal to count means append at the end.
Shift only the tail: `for (int k = count; k > i; k--) a[k] = a[k - 1];` then `a[i] = v;`
lessons.title: insertAt and its guard
concept: P1's `insertAt(index, kv)` allows index 0 through `listCount` inclusive: inserting AT the count is a legal append. Anything bigger returns false with no change.
lessons.challenge: Read `n`, `n` values, then `i` and `v`. If `i > n` print **false** and the unchanged list. Otherwise insert `v` at index `i` (shift right from the back), print **true** and the new list.

hints: Expansion: `int *b = new int[cap + 2];` copy loop, `delete[] a;`, `a = b;`, `cap += 2;`
Delete the OLD array before repointing, or you leak it. Never delete and then copy.
lessons.title: The expand pattern
concept: When P1's list is full, `expand()` allocates a bigger array, copies the old values over, deletes the old array, and repoints. The pointer swap order matters.
lessons.challenge: Start with a `new` array of capacity 3. Read values until **-1**; when full, expand capacity by **2** using the allocate-copy-delete-repoint pattern. Finish by printing `capacity=C count=N` and the values.

hints: Both add and insert start with the same guard: `if (cnt == cap) return false;`
printIt is `for (int i = 0; i < cnt; i++) cout << i << ": " << a[i] << "\n";` and deleteFirst mirrors your l20 code.

lessons.title: Boss: miniList
concept: Everything P1 part A needs in one class: dynamic array, count vs capacity, front insert with shifting, append, guarded delete.
lessons.challenge: Finish `miniList`. `add` appends (false when full), `insert` shifts right and places at the front (false when full), `deleteFirst` uses the reference-parameter idiom, `printIt` prints one `index: value` line per entry. The provided main drives it: even inputs are added, odd inputs are inserted.

hints: Adding `cap - 1` and taking `% cap` is the same as subtracting 1, but it can never produce a negative number.
return (x + 1) % cap;   and   return (x + cap - 1) % cap;
lessons.title: Wraparound with %
concept: P2's macros are the whole trick: `cListInc` is `(x + 1) % listCapacity` and `cListDec` is `(x + listCapacity - 1) % listCapacity`, which steps backward without ever going negative.
lessons.challenge: Write `int inc(int x, int cap)` and `int dec(int x, int cap)` using those exact formulas. Main reads `cap` and `x`, then prints `inc(x, cap)` and `dec(x, cap)` on separate lines.

hints: Each insert is one `first = (first + cap - 1) % cap;` followed by printing first.
The value lands AT the new first, so print after stepping, and the final line reuses the same variable.
lessons.title: first walks backward
concept: In P2, `insert()` is O(1): decrement `first` with wraparound and drop the value there. No shifting, ever.
lessons.challenge: Read `cap`, `first`, and `n`. Simulate `n` inserts: each one moves `first` one step backward with wraparound and prints where the value landed. Finish with `first=F`.

hints: Validity is about count, not capacity: a virtual index is good when `vi < count`.
The map is one expression: `(first + vi) % cap`.
lessons.title: virtualToPhysical
concept: The user of cList thinks in **virtual** indexes: 0 is the first item. Physically, virtual index `vi` lives at `(first + vi) % listCapacity`. This mapping is the heart of P2.
lessons.challenge: Read `cap`, `first`, `count`, and `q`. Then for each of `q` virtual indexes: print its physical index, or **bad** when the virtual index is not less than `count`.

hints: add places without moving first: `a[(first + cnt) % cap] = v; cnt++;` insert is dec-then-place.
printIt loops virtual indexes 0 to cnt-1 and prints `a[(first + vi) % cap]` for each. readAt is the same map behind a `vi < cnt` guard.

lessons.title: Boss: the ring
concept: P2 part A in miniature: `add` places at `(first + count) % cap`, `insert` walks `first` backward, and every read goes through the virtual-to-physical map. Nothing ever shifts.
lessons.challenge: Finish the `ring` class. `add(v)` appends at the physical end slot, `insert(v)` steps `first` backward and places there, `readAt(vi, v)` validates then maps, `printIt` prints `vi: value` in **virtual** order. The main drives it like the miniList boss, then does one `readAt`.

hints: Two lines of logic: `if (n == 0) return 0;` then the recursive case.
return n + sumTo(n - 1); trusts the smaller call to be right. That trust is the whole trick.
lessons.title: Recursion warm-up
concept: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem until it hits a base case. Every P4 tree function works this way.
lessons.challenge: Write `int sumTo(int n)` that returns 0 when `n` is 0, and otherwise returns `n + sumTo(n - 1)`. Main reads `n` and prints the sum of 1 through n.

hints: The deepest call is climb(0), which does nothing. Then climb(1) finishes and prints 1, then climb(2) prints 2, and so on back up.
void climb(int n) { if (n == 0) return; climb(n - 1); cout << n << "\n"; }
lessons.title: Work on the way back
concept: Code AFTER the recursive call runs while the calls unwind, in reverse order. In-order tree printing depends on placing work before, between, or after recursive calls.
lessons.challenge: Write `void climb(int n)` that prints nothing for 0, and otherwise calls `climb(n - 1)` FIRST and prints `n` on its own line AFTER. The result: 1 through n in ascending order, with no loop.

hints: Each node needs new: `tnode *root = new tnode; root->val = r;` then hook children onto root->left and root->right.
Print with arrows: `cout << root->left->val` reaches through the pointer. The last check is `if (root->left->left == nullptr)`.
lessons.title: A node points to nodes
concept: A tree node holds a value and two pointers to more nodes. An absent child is `nullptr`, and checking for it is the base case of every tree function.
lessons.challenge: Read three ints `r`, `a`, `b`. Build a root node holding `r`, give it a left child holding `a` and a right child holding `b` (grandchildren all null). Print the three values on separate lines, then print **null** if the left child's left pointer is null.

hints: The base case does three things: allocate, set val, null both children. Because t is a reference, that new node is now attached to the tree.
The recursive case is two lines: `if (v < t->val) insert(t->left, v); else insert(t->right, v);` The reference keeps working at every level down.
lessons.title: Recursive insert
concept: THE tree skill: `void insert(tnode *&t, int v)`. The `*&` means t IS the caller's pointer, so assigning a new node to a null t hooks it into the tree. Smaller goes left, otherwise right.
lessons.challenge: Write recursive `insert`. Base case: `t` is null, so make the node right there. Otherwise recurse left when `v < t->val`, else right. Main inserts values until **-1** and reports the root and its two children.

hints: Three statements between the base case and the closing brace, and their ORDER is the whole lesson: left call, cout, right call.
The null check comes first: `if (t == nullptr) return;` Every tree function you write this semester starts that way.
lessons.title: In-order traversal
concept: In-order means: all of the left subtree, then me, then all of the right subtree. On a BST that visits values in sorted order, which is how printIt works.
lessons.challenge: A working `insert` is provided. Write recursive `void printIt(tnode *t)`: return on null, recurse left, print `t->val` on its own line, recurse right. Main inserts until **-1** then calls it, and the output must come out sorted.

hints: Two base cases this time: null tree (false) and no-left-child (found it). Only one recursive case: go left.
if (t->left == nullptr) { m = t->val; return true; } return findMin(t->left, m); and never look right.
lessons.title: findMin
concept: The smallest value in a BST is the leftmost node: keep going left until there is no left. Remove() needs findMin later, so it gets its own function, in the course's bool-plus-reference style.
lessons.challenge: Write `bool findMin(tnode *t, int &m)` — a loop (as on the board) or recursion, your choice. Empty tree: return **false** without touching `m`. Otherwise store the leftmost value in `m` and return **true**. Main inserts until **-1**, then prints `min X` or `empty`.

hints: The public functions are one-liners: `void grove::insert(int v) { insertHelper(root, v); }` The helpers hold all the recursion, exactly like your l31-l32 code.
containsHelper has three outcomes: null is false, equal is true, otherwise recurse into the side v belongs on. Mind the const on both declaration and definition.
lessons.title: Boss: the grove
concept: The full P4 architecture in miniature: a class holding a private root, PUBLIC one-argument functions the user calls, each handing off to a PRIVATE recursive helper that takes the extra node pointer.
lessons.challenge: Finish `grove`. Public `insert(v)`, `contains(v)`, and `printIt()` each call their recursive private helper on `root`. Insert goes left on smaller, contains searches by comparing, printIt is in-order. Main inserts until **-1**, prints the tree sorted, then runs `contains` on every remaining input.

hints: The condition `cin >> p.key && cin >> p.value` is false at end of input, which stops the loop. This is exactly how the real driver reads.
Inside the loop: cout << "(" << p.key << "," << p.value << ")\n"; n++; and after it print the count line.
lessons.title: Read the driver
concept: The professor's test driver reads key-value pairs from input until it runs out, then drives your class. Understanding that loop is understanding how you will be graded.
lessons.challenge: A `kvpair` holds a key and a value. Read pairs until end of input using `while (cin >> p.key && cin >> p.value)`, print each as **(key,value)** on its own line (no spaces inside), then print **Pairs read: N**.

hints: Three cases now, and their order matters: null first (place), equal second (reject), then the two recursive sides. Compare `p.key` against `t->p.key`, never whole pairs.
The base case builds the node: t = new tnode; t->p = p; t->left = nullptr; t->right = nullptr; return true; and the duplicate case is one line: if (p.key == t->p.key) return false;

lessons.title: printIt, harness style
concept: The driver prints a count line, a header, then calls printIt, which must produce **(key,value)** pairs in ascending key order, one per line. In-order traversal does the sorting for free.
lessons.challenge: A duplicate-rejecting `insert` is provided. Write `void printIt(tnode *t)`: in-order, printing each node as **(key,value)** on its own line. The main prints **Tree count is N** and **Tree contents are:** first, exactly like the real driver.

hints: Mirror getValue's search shape: smaller keys recurse left, bigger recurse right, equal means you found the node to delete.
The delete pattern: tnode *old = t; then t = (t->left != nullptr) ? t->left : t->right; then delete old; return true; A leaf falls out of the same code because both children are null.

lessons.title: remove: leaf and one child
concept: Remove has three cases; today is the two easy ones. A **leaf** just gets deleted. A node with **one child** gets replaced by that child. The `tnode *&` reference is what makes the parent's pointer update automatically.
lessons.challenge: Write `bool remove(int key, tnode *&t)` handling: not found (false), leaf, and one-child nodes. The driver sweeps keys from **30 down to 10** counting successes, then prints **Delete Count is N** and the remaining contents. (Two-children nodes are next lesson; this data never needs that case.)

hints: Order the equal-key case: check for two children FIRST. Only fall through to the save-repoint-delete pattern when at most one child exists.

The two-children branch is exactly two lines: t->p = findMin(t->right); return remove(t->p.key, t->right); The node object stays; only its pair changes, and the duplicate down in the right subtree gets removed.

lessons.title: remove: two children
concept: The hard case: a node with **two** children can't just vanish. Copy the **minimum of the right subtree** into it (the smallest key that is still bigger than everything on the left), then remove that minimum from the right subtree. That minimum has no left child, so removing it is always an easy case.
lessons.challenge: `findMin` is provided (your l33 skill, now returning a `kvpair`). Extend `remove` with the two-children case: copy `findMin(t->right)` into `t->p`, then `return remove(t->p.key, t->right)`. The driver sweeps keys **60 down to 20**, then prints the survivors.

hints: getValue is your l34 containsHelper with one extra assignment before the true. The probe loop finds hits in ascending order automatically because it counts upward.
clear must recurse BEFORE delete: clear(t->left); clear(t->right); delete t; t = nullptr; Because t is a reference, the caller's pointer really becomes null.

lessons.title: getValue and clear
concept: Two more graded functions. `getValue` is the bool-plus-reference search: found means fill the reference and return true. `clear` deletes every node **post-order**: both children first, then the node itself, so you never delete a node while still needing its pointers.
lessons.challenge: Write `bool getValue(int key, int &value, tnode *t)` and `void clear(tnode *&t)` (clear must leave `t` null). The driver probes **even keys 0 to 98** printing **getValue reports this is in the list: (key,value)** for hits, clears, then prints **The cleared tree status:  count = 0** (two spaces!) using a recount.

hints: Every public function is one line delegating to its helper on root. nCount changes in exactly three places: insertHelper's base case (up), removeHelper's delete branch (down), and clear (to zero).
Careful with remove's two-children case and nCount: the recursive removeHelper call on the right subtree already decrements it there, so the two-children branch itself must not touch nCount.

concept: Everything the real driver does, in one run: read pairs rejecting duplicates, count and print, sweep-delete, count and print again, probe with getValue, clear, and prove the tree is empty. The provided main follows the professor's driver phase for phase, format string for format string.

hints: Override syntax: the same signature as the base, plus the word override. Inside it, `grove::insert(p)` runs the base version. That's the whole idea from class: BST::insert(p), then your extra step.

lessons.title: The base class
concept: A class can be built on top of another class and reuse everything in it. The base class marks the functions it is willing to let a derived class replace as virtual, keeps what the derived class needs in a protected area, and the derived class overrides a function by doing the base's work first and then adding its own step. This is exactly how the balanced tree (P5) will be built on the BST (P4).
lessons.challenge: Complete `agrove`, a class built on `grove`, by overriding `insert`. Call `grove::insert(p)` to do the real work; if it returns **true**, print one line: `insert K: count N, height H, balanced` (or `UNBALANCED`), using the protected `nCount` directly and the provided `height()` and `balanced()`. Return what the base returned. Main holds the object through a `grove &`; because `insert` is virtual, your version still runs.

hints: A leaf has no children, so calcHeight gives 1 + max(0, 0) = 1. That's why the professor's output shows leaves at height 1 and an empty tree at 0.

insertHelper is the l42 pattern exactly: base first, then your step. Because grove's helper recurses through the virtual function, bal(t) runs at every node on the way back up — you never write a loop to fix all the heights.

lessons.title: AVL: heights
concept: A balanced tree needs to know how tall every subtree is. Each node stores its height (a leaf is 1, an empty tree is 0), the height is recomputed at every node on the way back up the recursion, and the derived class does that by calling the base helper first and then bal(t). Rotations come next lesson; this one is the measuring tape.
lessons.challenge: Complete `agrove`'s four functions: `height(t)` returns 0 for an empty tree, else `t->h`. `calcHeight(t)` returns 1 + the taller child's height (use `max`). `bal(t)` (no rotations yet): if `t` is real, set `t->h = calcHeight(t)`. `insertHelper` overrides the base: call `grove::insertHelper(p, t)`, then `bal(t)`, return what the base returned. Main inserts pairs then prints `At i the value is (k,v): height = h` in order — the real P5 format.

hints: Order inside a rotation matters: move the middle subtree first, then hang t1 under t2, then recompute heights bottom-up (t1 before t2), and only then assign t1 = t2 through the reference.

The kink test: left heavy, but height(t->left->left) < height(t->left->right) → the weight is in the inner grandchild. rotateLeft(t->left) first straightens it into a plain left-left case; then rotateRight(t) fixes it.

lessons.title: Boss: rotations
concept: When an insert or remove leaves a node two levels heavier on one side, one or two rotations fix it locally: a right rotation for a left-heavy node, a left rotation for a right-heavy one, with the opposite rotation on the child first when the heaviness is a kink. Done at every node on the unwind, this keeps the tree's height near log n — which is the entire point.
lessons.challenge: Write `rotateRight`, `rotateLeft`, and the balancing branches of `bal`. `rotateRight(t1)`: `t1` is left heavy — its left child `t2` takes its place: `t1->left = t2->right; t2->right = t1;` then fix `t1->h` and `t2->h` (in that order) and set `t1 = t2`. `rotateLeft` is the mirror. `bal(t)`: if `!doBal` just set the height; otherwise compare `height(t->left)` and `height(t->right)`: a difference of 2 means rotate — and if the heavy child leans the *other* way (a kink), rotate that child the opposite direction first. Main runs the professor's full P5 protocol; test 1 must match his `AVLcorrectOutput` exactly.
